newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptians find gold necklace awarded in 1500 BC.
newsitem.headline: Egyptians find gold necklace awarded in 1500 BC.

text.p: Egyptian archaeologists working in the Nile Delta have found a necklace of golden flies thought to be a military decoration awarded by the Pharaoh Ahmose over 3,500 years ago, a government newspaper said on Wednesday.
The necklace, with 19 pendants in the shape of flies, turned up in excavations at Tell Basta, an important site about 70 km (45 miles) northeast of Cairo, the newspaper al-Ahram reported.

The archaeologists found it alongside a cartouche inscribed with the name of Ahmose, the founder of the dynasty which later brought ancient Egypt to the peak of its power and prosperity. The pharaoh ruled from 1570 to 1546 BC.

The head of the archaeological mission, Mahmoud Omar, speculated that the owner of the necklace won it for military service against the Hyksos, Asian invaders expelled by Ahmose after they had ruled northern Egypt for 200 years.
The newspaper quoted him as saying this type of fly necklace was characteristic of Ahmose's times but examples do exist from other periods in the history of pharaonic Egypt.
The newspaper published a colour photograph of the necklace. Neither Amr nor antiquities officials in Cairo were available give more details about the discovery.
Tell Basta is best known for its cemetery of mummified cats, associated with the local cat goddess Bastet. It was also an important garrison town on the eastern frontier of the Delta.
